idiom_name: native bool + operator true/operator false (or a named predicate)
implementation_notes: C# already enforces the pattern's invariant: bool is a distinct type with no standard conversions to or from the integral types, conditions require a boolean, and `true + 1` or `b == 1` are compile errors. A domain type becomes testable either through a named predicate (`public bool IsEmpty()`, the default recommendation) or through the pairwise `public static bool operator true(T x)` / `operator false(T x)`, which make it usable in `if`, `while`, `do`, `for` and ternary conditions without adding an implicit bool conversion; short-circuit `&&`/`||` additionally require matching `operator &`/`operator |`. Avoid declaring `implicit operator bool`: it makes the object convertible in every context, not just conditions, for no extra safety.
pitfalls: `true` and `false` must be declared pairwise (a compile error otherwise), and short-circuiting over a custom type also requires `operator &`/`operator |` with the semantics the spec mandates.

An `implicit operator bool` takes precedence over `operator true`/`operator false` in most contexts and reopens the type to every conversion site, including overload resolution - declare it only if a boolean-like object everywhere is really wanted.
`bool?` is not `bool`: conditions on a nullable boolean need `== true`, `?? false` or `GetValueOrDefault()`, so a nullable flag silently converts an intended test into a nullability question.
